issues.explanation: These trigger items are hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type of a 41-year-old male relief worker in a war zone. 'When people say things like my ex' implies a breakup/relationship-themed trauma context that is not reflected anywhere in the memory or appraisal items. 'Being naked' likewise suggests a sexual/interpersonal vulnerability cue, but the rest of the profile centers on shame, moral injury, and reliving tied to war-zone experiences rather than sexual trauma. The time-of-day trigger is coherent, but these two triggers pull toward a different trauma narrative and are not supported by the other selected items or formulation-linked nodes.

'Being naked' is a hard-to-explain trigger in the context of a relief worker in a war zone when the rest of the profile centers on morally injurious recollection, shame, and value-based self-appraisal. The other triggers (time of day, alcohol smell) plausibly connect to war-zone scenes and cue vivid reliving, but this item introduces a markedly different vulnerability/sexual-exposure theme that is unsupported by the memory and appraisal items, making the trigger set less clinically coherent with the trauma type and the formulation.

vignette:
Kenji moves with a precision that seems at odds with the chaos he now carries inside him. At forty-one, his body is still the finely tuned instrument of a professional dancer, capable of expressing nuance and strength in a single, fluid line. This control, however, stops at the threshold of his own mind. Six months ago, he returned from a three-month stint as a relief worker, a decision born from a desire to use his physical discipline for something beyond the stage. He was stationed at a temporary field clinic in a war-torn region, and it was there, in the late afternoon sun, that his life fractured. The clinic was hit by a mortar. The memory of it is not a coherent narrative but a series of sensory shards: the sudden, deafening roar; the smell of burning plastic and something sickeningly sweet; the sight of dust and splintered wood raining down. Just before the attack, the small team had been sharing a bottle of cheap, harsh whiskey, a fleeting moment of camaraderie that now feels like a damning indictment.

The past does not stay in the past. It erupts into the present without warning, often at the dance studio he co-owns with his husband. The smell of a celebratory glass of wine after a successful rehearsal can send him reeling. In an instant, he is no longer surrounded by mirrors and cheering colleagues but is back in the choking dust of the clinic, the scent of alcohol thick in the air just before the explosion. When the memories come, he feels the rumble in the floorboards as if it is happening right now, his muscles tensing for an impact that never arrives. He is left trembling, the applause of his dancers sounding distant and muffled, like sounds heard from underwater. This sudden reliving of the event is often followed by a wave of intense shame, a feeling that washes over him and leaves him cold and exposed, even in a warm, crowded room.

These moments of recall serve as fresh evidence for a set of harsh truths he has come to believe about himself. When he remembers freezing for a split second amidst the chaos, that image confirms his deepest fear: that he acted in a way that goes against his own values, the values of a helper, a protector. The memory doesn't just haunt him; it convicts him, reinforcing the belief that he is a ‘lousy coper’ who failed the only test that ever truly mattered. He looks at his life now—his inability to be present with his husband, his sudden panic in the studio—and sees only proof that he cannot rely on himself. This searing judgment is not just a consequence of the memories; it is also their cause.

In quieter moments, when the day’s work is done, this belief that he is fundamentally broken becomes its own kind of torment. Lying in bed, unable to sleep, he will find himself deliberately replaying the event. His self-loathing acts as a magnet for the memory, pulling it forward as he relentlessly sifts through the details, searching for the exact moment of his failure, punishing himself with the replay. This internal prosecution also makes the external world feel fraught with danger. Because he is so convinced of his inability to cope, he is constantly scanning his environment for things that might set him off. As the clock ticks past 4 PM each day, a familiar tension coils in his stomach. The afternoon light, once a source of warmth, now feels ominous, and he finds himself anticipating the smell of a neighbor’s barbecue or a passing car’s exhaust, bracing for the inevitable sensory ambush that his own vigilance seems to invite.

The cycles have tightened over the months, isolating him from his husband and his art. The grace and control he commands on stage have become a desperate performance, a mask for the terror and self-recrimination that churn within. He came to therapy after a dress rehearsal where the smell of burnt rosin, a scent he once associated with his craft, triggered a full-blown panic attack, leaving him gasping for air on the side of the stage. He is terrified that he is losing the one part of himself he still recognizes—the dancer. He feels trapped in the wreckage of that single afternoon, and he is desperate to find a way out before he disappears into it completely.
